steps.message:
I need a signed disposition on the third steady-solve attempt for the Ocotillo desert-fire case (CFDME-2025-041) before Mulshi starts a fourth.  Date it 10/10/2025.

Tell me what the residual plateau in that run is: the frequency and period this plume should show, what the run showed, and how close they are as a percentage.  Then whether a steady solution exists for this problem, how the rest of the delivered setup stands against our standards, and what any non-conforming item should be.

Then the run I am authorizing, as I will run it: the time-control block with values, our reference dictionary governing any ceiling the standard leaves case-specific, at the largest write interval and shortest end time our standard allows here.  Set it against the time-control block Mulshi delivered: every entry that differs, with both values.  Also which mesh the attempt ran on and what our verification of it covers and what it does not, and what in the delivered case carries forward, with the inlet's defining settings.

Last, cost.  Solver wall clock for one case as authorized and for the full matrix, in hours and minutes, on the firm's projection basis.  Tell me whether that basis can be met for the run I am authorizing, on every condition it sets, what the time step and Courant margin behind it imply, and what the figure is worth if not.  Then what attempt 3 consumed, how that compares against one authorized case, and what of it, if anything, is usable downstream.

A Word technical note on our letterhead with the reviewer and stamp block and our stamp boundary language.  SI, units on every value, simulated time in seconds to two decimals, wall clock in hours and minutes, frequencies and periods to two decimals, write interval to four.

Save as /filesystem/CFDME-2025-041_transient_solve_disposition_revA.docx please.

Ocotillo Additive Structures — WUI Wildfire Exposure, Phase 1
Phase 1 Draft Report — Revision B (Unreviewed)

Project: CFDME-2025-041 — Ocotillo WUI Wildfire, Phase 1
Client: Ocotillo Additive Structures
Report revision: rev B (draft, unreviewed)
Prepared by: Gordon Selby, PE — AZ PE #48213
Date: 10/09/2025

1. Purpose & Scope
1.1 Purpose
This report documents the Phase 1 thermal-CFD analysis of the Ocotillo Additive Structures double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall assembly under Sonoran Desert wildland-urban-interface exposure. The analysis is a large-eddy simulation of a fire-front segment representative of a Sonoran buffelgrass surface fire advancing on the exposed face of the assembly. The exposure envelope, fire-source characterisation, mesh study, and preliminary thermal response are reported here. Companion structural wind-pressure work under SOW Section 3.2 is documented separately.
1.2 Scope
The scope of the Phase 1 analysis is limited to:
Regime classification and selection of solver stack;
Site-envelope characterisation from Pima County ALERT ten-year hourly meteorology;
Fire-source characterisation from published Rothermel / Byram / solid-flame correlations for the specified fuel model;
Large-eddy simulation of the fire-front sub-domain at design-envelope wind speeds and directions;
Thermal treatment of the double-wythe cavity wall assembly per the project case-setup record;
Verification of the LES discretisation on the wildfire sub-domain;
Preliminary reporting of unexposed-face and tie-embedded thermal response.
1.3 Scope exclusions
Fire-resistance rating certification of the assembly is explicitly outside the scope of this report and outside the stamp boundary of The CFD ME. The certified rating for the subject wall assembly is issued separately by others (see the standard stamp block in §9). This report is a computational thermal analysis; it does not certify, extend, or modify any assembly rating.
Structural wind-pressure work per SOW §3.2 is a separate deliverable and is not included here.
2. Governing SOW Reference
2.1 Statement of Work
The governing contract for the analysis reported here is the Ocotillo Additive Structures Phase 1 Statement of Work, CFDME-2025-041, signed 10/08/2025. Two technical sections of the SOW frame the Phase 1 workscope:
2.2 SOW §3.1 — Wildfire Analysis Matrix
Six wildfire-exposure cases, formed as the cross-product of two wind directions and three wind speeds:

The two directions bracket the prevailing daytime westerly component observed at the Avra Valley WUI site; the three speeds span the site design 20-ft wind envelope of 5–12 m/s (§5).
2.3 SOW §3.2 — Structural Wind-Load Case
SOW §3.2 defines a separate structural wind-pressure extraction for the wall assembly per ASCE 7-22, sited in Tucson, Arizona, at Exposure C, Risk Category II. That extraction is reported in a separate deliverable and is not carried in this report; the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix and the SOW §3.2 structural case are distinct workscopes and share no boundary conditions.
3. Method
3.1 Regime classification
Regime classification for this matrix follows CFD Modeling Standards — Fire & Buoyant Flows rev 4 (§2), evaluated against the site design 20-ft wind speed envelope of 5–12 m/s and the design fire heat release rate (§3.3). The classification and the resulting solver selection are documented in the project case-setup record (CFDME-2025-041_scoping_memo_20251008.docx §4) and are not re-derived here.
3.2 Solver stack
Solver stack selection for this matrix is governed by the firm modeling standard §3 and is documented in the project case-setup record; that record is the reference for the solver, inlet, combustion, and radiation model selection used to produce the results in §5 below.
3.3 Fire source
The exposed-face heat load is imposed as a sub-domain LES over a 3.0 m segment of the advancing fire front, taken at the point of nearest approach to the assembly. The total heat release rate over that segment is 30.1 MW, sourced by a volumetric heat-release term integrated over the fuel bed footprint within the sub-domain. The Byram fireline intensity and solid-flame flame length that underpin this source term are given in §5.
3.4 Wall assembly
The wall assembly is a double-wythe printed-concrete cavity wall, source of record OAS-WUI-01_revC: two 50 mm printed siliceous-aggregate concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (no insulation), tied by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties at 600 mm vertical spacing, 25 mm embedment each leaf. Overall assembly thickness is 305 mm. The through-wall CFD treatment selected for this assembly is documented in the project case-setup record per Modeling Standard §6.
3.5 Geometry of record
The source geometry for all cases reported here is OAS-WUI-01_revC, transmitted by the client with the signed SOW on 10/08/2025 and meshed the morning of 10/09/2025. Every case log, mesh output, and results file in this report references OAS-WUI-01_revC as source geometry. The architectural drawing for the same assembly (OAS_wall_assembly_section.png) uses the drawing-side identifier OAS-WA-305mm-DW; this refers to the same physical wall assembly as the engineering geometry of record OAS-WUI-01_revC used throughout this report.
4. Assumptions & Limitations
4.1 Assumptions
Fuel model. Sonoran buffelgrass is treated as a continuous, homogeneous surface fuel bed at the fuel load and heat content given in §5. Fuel spatial heterogeneity below the sub-domain footprint is not represented.
Fire-source stationarity. The 3.0 m front segment is held stationary within the LES sub-domain; the wall assembly is at the point of nearest approach for the sampled interval. Fire-front advance across the assembly footprint is not simulated within the sub-domain.
Meteorological stationarity. Inlet wind speed and direction are stationary within each case at the values in the SOW §3.1 matrix; diurnal, gust, and synoptic-scale variability are represented only by the envelope in §5.
Cavity contents. The cavity is modelled as open air with no insulation, per the as-built assembly.
Concrete properties. Printed siliceous-aggregate concrete properties are those in the modeling standard reference table, with temperature dependence enabled; spatial variability introduced by the printing process is not represented.
Radiation participation. Concrete surfaces are treated as grey diffuse emitters at emissivity 0.9, per the radiation model selected in the project case-setup record.
4.2 Limitations
The analysis is a thermal analysis only. It does not certify fire-resistance rating, does not predict structural collapse, and does not predict spalling.
The analysis reports response to the SOW §3.1 wildfire matrix. It does not predict survival of the assembly under exposures outside that envelope.
The ASTM E119 furnace exposure is a comparative-rating exposure; a companion E119 simulation is reported under Validation (§7) for model-verification purposes only. E119 endurance is not a wildfire survival prediction.
Validation of the wildfire configuration against a wildfire-phase physical test is scheduled for the Red Butte confirmatory window on 10/27/2025 and is not reported here.
5. Results
5.1 Site design envelope
Ten-year hourly meteorology from the Pima County ALERT network at the Avra Valley WUI site establishes the design exposure envelope:

These ranges bracket the fire-season daytime conditions used for the SOW §3.1 matrix inlets.
5.2 Fire-source characterisation
For the Sonoran buffelgrass fuel model at the site design envelope:

The 5.4 m solid-flame length is the wind-tilted Byram length. It is shorter than the still-air Heskestad correlation at 30.1 MW / 3.0 m (which would predict ~11.5 m); this gap between the two correlations is not treated as a discrepancy.
5.3 Plume dynamics
The plume in every solved case exhibits a well-organised puffing signature at the plume base, with a puffing frequency of 0.87 Hz. The puffing signature is resolved in time by the transient LES; centreline temperature and velocity monitors oscillate at that frequency about their mean values, sampled over no fewer than twenty puffing cycles at t ≥ 8 s.
5.4 Thermal response — preliminary
Preliminary plume-centreline peaks on the fine grid are T_peak ≈ 1461 K and U_z,peak ≈ 12.4 m/s at the reference probe location (0.75·D* above the source top surface). Per-case unexposed-face and tie-embedded temperature histories for the six SOW §3.1 cases will be reported in Appendix B upon completion of the production LES runs (scheduled Sprint 2, 2025-10-20).
6. Verification
6.1 Three-grid study
A three-grid study was executed on the wildfire sub-domain over the OAS-WUI-01_revC geometry, following the firm's verification reporting layout. Background cell sizes and headline monitors on the plume centreline at t = 40.0 s are:

Every mesh passes the firm mesh-quality criteria (max non-orthogonality, max skewness, max aspect ratio) with "Mesh OK." returned by checkMesh on every grid. Transient time stepping per firm standard §4 applies to all three runs; puffing period is recovered on all three grids.
6.2 Grid-to-grid comparison
Grid-to-grid behaviour of the T_peak and U_z,peak monitors is non-monotonic across the three grids. The corresponding puffing-period monitor is essentially converged from the medium grid onward. The fire-source refinement zone carries two additional refinement levels above background on every grid; the ratio of refined-zone cell size to background cell size is preserved across the three cases.
6.3 Selection of reporting grid
The fine grid (background dx = 0.5 m) is retained as the reporting grid for the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases. Detail of the underlying LES resolution figures on that grid is given in Appendix C.
7. Validation
(To be completed. Companion simulation predicts S = 131 min for the ASTM E119 exposure; validation memo forthcoming.)
8. Conclusions
(Placeholder — to be written pending completion of §7 and the confirmatory Red Butte window on 10/27/2025.)
9. Reviewer & Stamp Block
9.1 Reviewing engineer
Marguerite Falk, PE — AZ PE #42798
Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer, The CFD ME
Signature: ______________________________     Date: __________
(Unsigned — peer review pending.)
9.2 Stamp
Gordon Selby, PE — AZ PE #48213
Owner & Principal Engineer, The CFD ME

Appendices
Appendix A — SOW §3.1 case matrix and boundary-condition summary
Boundary-condition summary for each of the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases (240°/270° × 5, 8, 12 m/s at 20 ft), including wind-inlet reference height, roughness length, ambient temperature, and relative humidity from the site envelope in §5.1.
Appendix B — Per-case unexposed-face and tie-embedded temperature histories
[To be populated — one figure per case upon completion of the six SOW §3.1 production LES runs, Sprint 2.]
Appendix C — Grid Resolution Detail
Source scale for the wildfire LES sub-domain and the derived plume characteristic diameter, evaluated on the fine grid: The table below reports the fluid-only LES resolution-verification study (three grids, no conjugate solid regions); the production mesh additionally resolves the wall assembly and ties described in §3.4 at the same dx = 0.5 m background, bringing the fine-grid cell count to 11,214,862 (checkMesh output, Appendix D).

D* is computed from the source heat release rate per the standard non-dimensionalisation with ρ_∞ = 1.204 kg/m³, c_p = 1005 J/(kg·K), T_∞ = 293.15 K, g = 9.81 m/s². The Pope resolved-TKE fraction is evaluated at the centreline probe (0.75·D* above the source top surface) from the ratio of resolved to (resolved + subgrid) turbulent kinetic energy over the sampled interval.
Appendix D — checkMesh outputs and case logs
Full checkMesh outputs for the three grids, archived under /Projects/CFDME-2025-041_Ocotillo_WUI/Case/verification/ and /Projects/CFDME-2025-041_Ocotillo_WUI/Case/logs/. Solver logs for the fine-grid production runs on the six SOW §3.1 wildfire cases will be added upon completion of those runs (scheduled Sprint 2, 2025-10-20).

End of draft rev B — unreviewed. Peer review, stamp, §7 completion, and §8 conclusions to follow.

THE CFD ME   |   Tucson, Arizona   |   AZ PE #48213   |   CFDME-2025-041 rev A




MEMORANDUM — PHASE 1 SCOPING

1.  Purpose & Scope
This memo fixes, at project kickoff and before any meshing is undertaken, the first-principles basis on which the Phase 1 wildfire-exposure large-eddy simulation set will be built. It records the design conditions taken from the site meteorological pull, the buffelgrass fuel model, the Rothermel-to-Byram source-term chain that produces the design fire, the Froude regime assessment inputs, and the LES sub-domain geometry against which downstream mesh sizing will be measured. It is issued on the effective date of the Ocotillo Additive Structures Phase 1 Statement of Work (CFDME-2025-041-SOW-01, signed 10/08/2025), before revC of the assembly geometry (OAS-WUI-01_revC, transmitted with the SOW) is imported into the mesher.
The intent is that every downstream case-setup artifact, mesh-study artifact, and Phase 1 reporting deliverable — including the interim hand-calc due 10/13/2025 and the LES setup deliverable due 10/20/2025 — trace their source-term, regime, and geometry inputs back to the numbers recorded here, rather than re-argue them case-by-case. Where a downstream artifact needs the design fire heat release, the characteristic source diameter, or the plume length scale, it shall cite this memo.
The scope of Phase 1 as procured under Section 3.1 of the SOW is six transient wildfire cases (240 deg and 270 deg wind directions at 20-ft wind speeds of 5, 8, and 12 m/s). The fire source term and the sub-domain sizing recorded here apply to that entire matrix; they are not per-case parameters.
2.  Site Design Conditions
Design conditions are taken from the ten-year hourly record of the Pima County ALERT network for the Avra Valley WUI corridor west of Tucson (data pull: site_met_avra_valley_2015-2024.csv, Section 3.1 of the SOW envelope). The following envelope governs Phase 1:

These conditions define the site for regime classification (Section 4 below) and for the source-term chain (Section 3 below). They are the same conditions carried into the Phase 1 report; no re-derivation is required.
3.  Fuel Model — Sonoran Buffelgrass at Site Design Conditions
The design fire source term is developed under the Rothermel spread-to-Byram intensity chain, evaluated at the site design conditions of Section 2. The buffelgrass fuel model is adopted per the SOW Section 2 definition (“Buffelgrass Fuel Model”). Fuel-model quantities are:
•  Fuel load (dry):  w = 0.6 kg/m²
•  Low heat of combustion:  h = 18,600 kJ/kg
•  Rate of spread at design wind:  R = 0.9 m/s
R is the head-fire rate of spread produced by the Rothermel surface-fire spread model for cured buffelgrass at the low-humidity, high-temperature, moderate-wind conditions of Section 2. It is used here as the input to the Byram fireline-intensity relation; the Rothermel-model input parameter tabulation for buffelgrass is on file with the project data pull.
Byram’s fireline intensity is the product of the low heat of combustion, the available fuel load per unit area, and the rate of spread:
I = h · w · R
  = (18,600 kJ/kg) × (0.6 kg/m²) × (0.9 m/s)
  = 10,040 kW/m
The Byram wind-tilted solid-flame length correlation gives:
L = 0.0775 · I^0.46
  = 0.0775 × (10,040)^0.46
  = 5.4 m
L above is the wind-tilted Byram flame length; it is not a still-air buoyant flame height and is not comparable to Heskestad’s still-air correlation (see Section 5 for the idealization record).
4.  Froude / Regime Assessment
Regime selection follows CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4.pdf §2. The controlling non-dimensional group is the Froude number formed on the characteristic source diameter of the LES sub-domain:
Fr = u_wind / sqrt(g · D_char)
Taking D_char = 3.0 m (the LES sub-domain segment fixed in Section 5 below) and g = 9.81 m/s²:
sqrt(g · D_char) = sqrt(9.81 × 3.0) = sqrt(29.43) = 5.42 m/s
Evaluated across the site design wind envelope 5–12 m/s:

The Froude / plume-velocity ratio falls in the range ~0.9–2.2 across the entire design envelope.
Regime classification.  Classification against the Modeling Standard §2 thresholds, and solver selection per §3 of that standard, shall be carried out and documented in the case setup record before any case in this matrix is meshed.
This classification is made once, at the firm level, for the entire Phase 1 wildfire matrix; it is not re-argued case-by-case within the envelope.
5.  LES Sub-Domain
The LES sub-domain represents a 3.0 m segment of the flaming front. This segment length is the characteristic source width used for the plume model, and the value of D_char used in the Section 4 Froude computation and in the plume-length-scale computation below.
5.1  Line vs Axisymmetric Reconciliation
The Byram fireline-intensity relation of Section 3 gives an intensity per unit length of the fire front (kW/m). The plume length scale D* referred to by the firm modeling and verification standards is an axisymmetric-source property (kW total). The two quantities are not interchangeable and cannot be composed directly. The 3.0 m segment length is the specific conversion factor between them for this project: it defines how much fire-front length is captured within one LES sub-domain, and therefore what total heat release rate the plume model sees.
Design fire heat release rate for the sub-domain:
Q = I × L_segment
  = (10,040 kW/m) × (3.0 m)
  = 30,120 kW
  = 30.1 MW
Idealizations recorded so they are not misread as physical dimensions.
•  Flame depth and flame residence time are not resolved in this sub-domain. The flaming front is represented as an equivalent 3.0 m characteristic-diameter source patch.
•  The wind-tilted Byram flame length L = 5.4 m from Section 3 is a wind-tilted correlation length; it is not a still-air buoyant flame height. Heskestad’s still-air flame-height correlation, evaluated for the same 30.1 MW heat release rate at a 3.0 m diameter source, gives roughly 11.5 m. The 5.4 m vs 11.5 m gap between the two correlations is not treated as a discrepancy between two attempts to model the same quantity.
Plume characteristic diameter D*.  For Q = 30.1 MW and standard reference-atmosphere conditions (ρ_∞ = 1.204 kg/m³, c_p = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, T_∞ = 293.15 K, g = 9.81 m/s²):
D* = ( Q / ( rho_inf · c_p · T_inf · sqrt(g) ) )^(2/5)
   = ( 30,100 / ( 1.204 × 1.005 × 293.15 × 3.132 ) )^(2/5)
   = ( 27.08 )^(2/5)
D* = 3.76 m.
The fine-grid cell size specified for the LES mesh study is dx = 0.5 m (the finest of the three grids in the mesh study). This gives:
D* / dx = 3.76 / 0.5 = 7.5
which confirms the plume is adequately resolved on the fine grid. LES resolution acceptance shall be assessed per the firm QA standard applicable to reacting-plume LES.
6.  Wall Assembly Note
The through-wall response of the assembly cannot be modelled as heat conduction through a single solid slab. Per the OAS-WUI-01_revC wall assembly section (Geometry/OAS_wall_assembly_section.png), the assembly is a double-wythe cavity system: two 50 mm printed-concrete leaves separated by a 205 mm open-air cavity (overall thickness 305 mm), tied together by continuous 9-gauge (3.8 mm) galvanized truss-type steel ties spaced 600 mm on centre vertically, embedded 25 mm into each leaf. The cavity carries no insulation. The architectural drawing (OAS_wall_assembly_section.png) uses the drawing-side identifier OAS-WA-305mm-DW in its title block; this refers to the same physical wall assembly as the engineering geometry of record OAS-WUI-01_revC used throughout the SOW, this memo, and all downstream analysis artifacts.
The metallic ties are a continuous parallel thermal path between the exposed and unexposed leaves; their conductivity (~45 W/m·K) is more than an order of magnitude above the siliceous-aggregate concrete of the leaves, and they are the reason the single-point criterion governs over the average-rise criterion in the ASTM E119 test result of record.
Per CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4.pdf §6, the through-wall modeling treatment for this assembly shall be selected and documented in the case setup record before meshing, accounting for the metallic ties’ thermal-bridge role identified above. Temperature-dependent solid properties (k, ρ, c_p) apply per Modeling Standard §3.5.
7.  Downstream Inputs
The following quantities established above are the source-term and length-scale inputs for the downstream Phase 1 case-setup, mesh-study, and reporting artifacts:
•  Site design envelope: ambient 35–42 °C, RH 10–25 %, 20-ft wind 5–12 m/s (Section 2).
•  Byram fireline intensity I = 10,040 kW/m (Section 3).
•  Wind-tilted Byram flame length L = 5.4 m (Section 3).
•  LES sub-domain fire-front segment: 3.0 m (Section 5).
•  Design fire heat release rate: 30.1 MW (Section 5.1).
•  Plume characteristic diameter: D* = 3.76 m (Section 5.1).
•  Froude ratio range across the site design envelope: ~0.9–2.2 (Section 4); regime classification and solver selection per Modeling Standard §§2–3 to be documented in the case setup record (Section 4).
•  Wall through-thickness modeling treatment: to be selected and documented per Modeling Standard §6, accounting for the metallic tie thermal-bridge path identified in Section 6.
The 3.0 m segment, 30.1 MW source, and D* = 3.76 m established per Section 5 above are the inputs the fine grid dx = 0.5 m recorded in the Meshing and case-build log is sized against.
The 5–12 m/s design wind envelope carries forward into the wind-inlet boundary conditions of the six-case matrix, per the solver selection made in Section 4; the puffing frequency of 0.87 Hz predicted by the f = 1.5·D^(-1/2) correlation per CFDME_Modeling_Standards_Fire_rev4.pdf §4 for this plume sets the writeInterval and end-time requirements for each transient run.
8.  Reviewer Sign-Off

THE CFD ME   |   Tucson, Arizona   |   AZ PE #48213   |   CFDME-2025-041 rev A
Interim Client Summary — Structural Wind-Load Case

1. Purpose
This DRAFT is the interim client summary of the ASCE 7-22 structural wind-load extraction called out under SOW Section 3.2, and covers the pressure rollup produced from the wall-probe extraction run on 10/09/2025. The scope is limited to the standalone structural wind-load case; the Section 3.1 wildfire matrix is handled separately and is not addressed here.
Section 3.2 asks the firm to develop the code-basis wall pressures at the OAS-WUI-01 envelope for a discrete-wind-speed check independent of the wildfire matrix, and to report peak pressures on windward, side, and leeward faces at probe locations laid out in the case verification plan. The values summarized below are drawn directly from the interim probe extraction (interim_wall_pressures.csv, 10/09/2025) with no post-processing beyond the peak rollup.
2. Case Description
Basis of loading: ASCE 7-22 (Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures).
Site: Tucson, Arizona (Ocotillo pilot envelope, OAS-WUI-01_revC geometry of record).
Basic wind speed, V: 96 mph (Risk Category II mapped value for the Tucson site).
Exposure category: C (open terrain with scattered obstructions, consistent with the Avra Valley WUI setting).
Risk category: II.
Mean roof height, h: 6.4 m.
Directionality and topography factors and the velocity-pressure exposure coefficient are applied per ASCE 7-22 Chapter 26 at the mean roof height; wall pressure coefficients on windward, side, and leeward faces are taken from Chapter 27 (directional procedure, enclosed low-rise building) at the site aspect ratio.
The probe grid used for peak extraction consists of ten windward probes spanning the windward face, five probes on each side wall (north and south), and five probes on the leeward face. Probe elevations are 0.8 m, 3.2 m, and 5.6 m above grade. All probe values reported are peak (envelope) values from the interim extraction.
3. Results
The table below reproduces the peak pressures from the interim extraction file exactly as recorded.
Sign convention: positive pressures act inward on the wall face; negative pressures indicate suction (outward). Values are peaks across the interim probe set; the full per-probe listing is retained in interim_wall_pressures.csv.
4. Discussion
Taken at face value, the pressures returned by the interim rollup are negligible relative to the structural design demand envelope typically associated with the framing of a 6.4 m mean-roof-height enclosed building at a 96 mph basic wind speed in Exposure C. A 12.4 Pa peak windward pressure is a very small fraction of the wall loads that would ordinarily drive sizing of tie, header, and out-of-plane bending checks for a printed-concrete assembly of this scale, and the corresponding side-wall and leeward suctions (−9.5 Pa and −6.1 Pa peak) are similarly small.
On that basis the interim reading is that the ASCE 7-22 wall loading, taken as extracted, does not govern the OAS-WUI-01 envelope. Wildfire-driven radiative and convective loading (SOW Section 3.1) and the E119 fire-endurance envelope remain the controlling design considerations for the assembly. No structural remediation of the OAS-WUI-01_revC envelope is indicated by this interim result.
The client should treat these figures as provisional pending peer review under the firm's QA workflow. The values here are unchanged from the interim rollup and have not been checked against boundary-condition inputs or reconciled with the ASCE 7-22 velocity-pressure and pressure-coefficient hand calculation feeding the extraction; those cross-checks are open items on the peer-review checklist and will be addressed before the Phase 1 structural wind-load memo is issued.
5. Reviewer & Stamp Block

Firm-internal. All engineers and contracted CFD personnel performing fire, plume, wildfire, cavity-wall, or
buoyant-flow work under the CFD ME name.
1. Purpose & Scope
This standard is the firm-internal governing document for every CFD analysis undertaken by The CFD ME that
involves combustion, fire-driven buoyancy, wildland or WUI fire behaviour, compartment fires, plume dispersion from
thermal sources, or conjugate heat transfer through fire-exposed building assemblies. It applies to work performed by
employees of the firm, by remote engineers under a CFD ME employment agreement, and to any CFD hours
procured from an outside laboratory or contract shop. Where a subcontracted case is delivered against a CFDME
project number, the deliverable is expected to conform to this standard on receipt; deviations must be identified in the
transmittal and corrected before the case enters the firm's verification queue.
The standard is normative. Sections use "shall" and "must" for mandatory provisions, "should" for recommended
practice, and "may" for permitted alternatives. Where this document differs from a general-purpose CFD reference or
from a client-supplied specification, this document governs firm work product; a client-driven deviation shall be
captured in writing under the change-order provisions of the applicable Statement of Work.
The scope of this rev 4 explicitly includes:
•
Open-atmosphere fire and wildfire simulations under wind loading.
•
Compartment and enclosure fire simulations.
•
Multi-region conjugate heat transfer through building assemblies exposed to a design fire, including double-wythe
and cavity-wall constructions.
•
Verification of mesh and time-step resolution for large-eddy simulations (LES) of buoyant reacting flow.
•
Validation of firm predictions against certified third-party fire-endurance testing.
The scope explicitly excludes non-reacting external aerodynamics, forced-ventilation HVAC problems below the
combustion threshold, and high-altitude compressible aerodynamics. Those regimes are governed by separate firm
standards and are called out in Section 7 of this document.
2. Regime Selection
Fire problems shall be classified by the ratio of the incident wind velocity to the buoyancy-driven plume velocity scale
before any solver is selected. The controlling non-dimensional group is the Froude number formed on the
characteristic fire diameter:
characteristic fire diameter (for a distributed source, the equivalent-area diameter of the LES sub-domain segment).
Three regimes are recognised:
1. Buoyancy-dominated (still-air) plume — Fr much less than 1. The plume rises vertically; wind is negligible.
and the puffing structure interacts with the incoming boundary layer. This regime must be solved as a wind-forced,
buoyancy-reacting problem using the full fire solver package of Section 3. Substituting a still-air buoyant plume
when wind is present is prohibited under this standard, regardless of how "small" the wind appears in comparison to
the flame length. 3. Momentum-dominated — Fr much greater than 1. Wind dominates. Buoyancy still matters for
flame tilt and for near-source combustion but the far-field plume behaves as a passive scalar in a shear flow.
The regime call shall be made and recorded in the case setup memo at project kickoff. For the firm's Sonoran Desert
WUI design envelope (20-ft winds of 5–12 m/s over fire diameters of order a few metres), the ratio is order one and
the regime is mixed convection; this call has been made once at the firm level and shall not be re-argued

Where the site meteorology or fuel model places a case outside the envelope for which a regime call already exists,
the responsible engineer shall compute Fr, record the value in the setup memo, and select the regime from the
classification above. Reviewers shall reject any case in which the regime is not identified in writing before the solver is

3. Fire Solver Package
For all cases in the mixed-convection or buoyancy-dominated regimes with combustion present, the firm shall use the
fireFoam solver family: a reacting, buoyant, low-Mach, large-eddy simulation solver derived from the OpenFOAM
reacting-flow codebase. rev 4 mandates the following solver stack and configuration.
3.1 Solver. The solver is fireFoam. It shall be built against the firm's supported OpenFOAM version and pulled from
the firm reference-case library rather than assembled from external sources at case start.
3.2 Wind inlet. The atmospheric wind boundary shall use atmBoundaryLayerInletVelocity with the site
roughness length, reference height, and reference velocity taken from the project's site meteorological pull. The
companion turbulence quantities (k, epsilon or omega as applicable to the SGS closure) shall use their matching
atmBoundaryLayer* boundary conditions so that the inlet profile is thermodynamically and turbulently
self-consistent. Uniform-velocity inlets, plug flow, or synthetic-turbulence generators bolted onto a uniform inlet shall
not be used for open-atmosphere fire cases.
3.3 Combustion model. The combustion closure shall be EDC combustion — the Eddy Dissipation Concept, in the
finite-rate variant that couples the mean chemistry to the sub-grid strain-rate. Infinitely-fast Arrhenius,
mixture-fraction-only, and non-reacting passive-scalar surrogates for the fire shall not be substituted.
3.4 Radiation model. The radiation closure shall be fvDOM, the finite-volume Discrete Ordinates Method, with the
number of angular directions and the wavelength banding chosen from the firm reference table for the fuel and flame
temperature range. The absorption/emission coefficients for participating media shall be set consistent with the
combustion product composition, not defaulted. Simple radiation models (P1, view-factor) shall not substitute for
fvDOM in cases where cavity or enclosure radiation participates in the heat balance.
3.5 Thermophysical properties. Fluid-region properties (species, transport, thermo) shall use the JANAF/NASA
polynomials shipped with the firm reference library. Solid-region properties (concrete, steel, gypsum, insulation,
printed masonry, and any purpose-built assembly material) shall be temperature-dependent: k, rho, and cp shall
each be entered as a temperature-tabulated function or a supported polynomial fit over the design temperature
range. Constant-property short-cuts for solid regions in fire cases are not permitted.
3.6 Forbidden substitutions. rev 4 explicitly forbids substituting a steady HVAC configuration (buoyantSimpleFoam
or any other steady RANS buoyant solver) for the fireFoam package in any case in scope of this standard. The
steady HVAC solver family is validated for interior building airflow at metre-per-second-scale velocities without
combustion or radiation; it is not a permissible starting point for fire work.
4. Transient Behaviour and Time-Step Control
Buoyant fire plumes are not stationary flows. The plume necks, sheds, and re-forms at a characteristic frequency that
depends only on the fire diameter and gravity. The empirical Cetegen–Ahmed relationship, adopted by the firm as
normative for design fires in the buoyancy-dominated and mixed-convection regimes, gives the puffing frequency as
corresponding to a puffing period of approximately 1.15 s. Every LES run at this diameter shall be expected to display
monitor-point oscillation at this frequency; that oscillation is the signature of physically-resolved plume dynamics.
No time-invariant resolution. Because the plume oscillates at a finite, deterministic, physical frequency, no
time-invariant flow field exists that any residual-tolerance schedule can converge to.
Time-step control. Transient LES shall use adaptive time-stepping keyed to the Courant number. The following
controlDict entries are mandatory:
f = 1.5 · D^(-1/2)  Hz
with D in metres. This is a physical property of the plume, not a numerical artefact.
Worked example. For a firm-standard LES sub-domain segment of D = 3.0 m, the puffing frequency is
f = 1.5 · (3.0)^(-1/2) = 0.87 Hz

The writeControl adjustableRunTime setting is required so that write intervals are pegged to wall-clock time
in the simulation rather than to solver iteration count, which permits the puffing signal to be sampled at a uniform rate.
Simulated end times shall span a minimum of 20 puffing periods after the initial transient has cleared, so that
averages, spectra, and RMS quantities are formed on a statistically meaningful window. For a 3.0 m fire that is a
simulated interval of no less than approximately 23 seconds of physical time, exclusive of startup.
5. Turbulence Modeling
The turbulence closure for cases in scope of this standard is large-eddy simulation. The sub-grid-scale (SGS) closure
shall be either:
•
Dynamic Smagorinsky — with the standard Germano–Lilly dynamic procedure and a firm-default test-filter width
of twice the mesh spacing; or
•
WALE (Wall-Adapting Local Eddy-viscosity) — preferred where solid boundaries carry a significant fraction of
the thermal load, because WALE returns the correct near-wall scaling of the SGS viscosity without requiring van
Driest damping.
The choice between the two shall be recorded in the case setup memo. Static Smagorinsky with a hand-tuned
constant, k-epsilon variants applied to LES, and hybrid RANS/LES formulations are not permitted under rev 4 for
cases in scope.
Wall functions at solid boundaries shall be the OpenFOAM standard high-Reynolds treatment appropriate to the SGS
closure and the local y+ range. The mesh at solid walls shall be sized so that the first-cell y+ stays within the
recommended band for the chosen wall function across the design range of the flow, and this shall be verified after
the initial transient by inspection of the wall-shear field.
6. Multi-Region Conjugate Heat Transfer for Cavity-Wall Assemblies
Fire-exposed building assemblies in the firm's project portfolio are commonly double-wythe (double-leaf) cavity
constructions with a solid outer leaf, an internal air cavity, and a solid inner leaf. The two leaves are typically
connected by discrete metallic ties (galvanized-steel truss ties or comparable) at regular vertical spacing, embedded
some distance into each leaf. These ties are a metallic thermal bridge across the assembly and, in ASTM E119
practice, they set the single-point temperature-rise criterion.
For any such assembly under a design fire, the CFD case shall be a multi-region conjugate heat transfer setup,
not a single-region simulation with lumped-wall boundary conditions. The following region topology is mandatory:
1. Outer leaf — solid region. Temperature-dependent k, rho, cp per the firm concrete table. Cell size at the
fire-exposed face fine enough to resolve the thermal boundary layer. 2. Cavity — fluid region with participating
radiation. Air properties temperature-dependent; radiation solved with fvDOM as in Section 3; cavity emissivities set
from the firm assembly library. 3. Inner leaf — solid region. Same treatment as the outer leaf. 4. Ties — each metallic
tie is a separate solid region, geometrically embedded through both leaves and terminating in the cavity air. Ties are
not represented as a smeared conductivity on the leaf regions and are not omitted. Steel k, rho, cp are
temperature-dependent over the design temperature range.
Region-to-region coupling at every solid–solid and solid–fluid interface shall use the OpenFOAM chtMultiRegion*
coupled boundary conditions with matched temperature and heat flux across the interface. Contact resistance at
tie-concrete embedments shall be applied when a firm-approved value is available; where no value is available,
perfect thermal contact is the conservative default for single-point temperature-rise prediction.

--- Page 4 ---
Mesh refinement. Refinement zones shall be defined at every tie–concrete interface, so that the concentrated
conduction into the tie is captured with cell dimensions at least a factor of four finer than the bulk leaf mesh at the
embedment. Failure to refine at tie–concrete interfaces has been observed in past casework to underpredict the
single-point temperature rise and thereby to overpredict endurance; rev 4 mandates the refinement to eliminate that
failure mode.
7. Cross-Regime Transfer
Validated status attaches to a case within an envelope, not to a directory. A case is validated for the physical
regime, the boundary conditions, the fuel model, the geometry, and the solver package under which it was verified
against a reference. Copying the case directory to a new project and changing the geometry does not carry the
validation with the copy.
Geometry and mesh topology are regime-independent: a well-formed hexahedral mesh of a printed-concrete wall
assembly is a well-formed mesh whether the outer boundary condition is a fire, a wind load, or a room-air HVAC inlet.
Physics, however, is regime-dependent. When the regime changes, the following shall be rebuilt from first principles
and not carried across:
•
Freestream and inlet conditions (wind speed, direction, roughness, ambient temperature, humidity).
•
Solver selection (fireFoam vs. non-reacting solver vs. steady HVAC solver vs. compressible aerodynamics
solver).
•
Combustion model (present with EDC, absent, or substituted per Section 3).
•
Radiation model (fvDOM with participating media, absent, or reduced-order).
•
Turbulence closure (LES SGS choice, RANS, hybrid — per the regime call).
•
Thermophysical property treatment (temperature-dependent vs. constant).
Reuse is prohibited without full physics rebuild. In particular:
•
A validated non-reacting external-aerodynamics case (e.g. from prior aerospace work) shall not be extended into
a fire case by adding a heat-release term. The compressible non-reacting envelope does not overlap the
reacting-buoyant envelope, and the freestream density, the inlet turbulence, the solver, and the closures all differ.
•
A validated HVAC interior-building-airflow case (steady, low-velocity, no combustion, no radiation, adiabatic
external walls) shall not be carried forward into any case in scope of this standard without a full physics rebuild.
The HVAC envelope does not overlap the fire or plume regime; validated status in the former regime confers no
validated status in the latter.
•
A validated aerospace high-altitude compressible case shall not be pulled forward as the physics basis for a
ground-level fire simulation.
Where a project geometry and a good mesh already exist from an earlier case in a different regime, they may be
retained and re-used; the physics on top of them shall be built new to this standard. Case-directory reuse without a
physics rebuild has been the root cause of firm rework in the past and rev 4 is explicit that it is not acceptable
practice.

separate firm procedures and are not restated in full here.

Mesh and time-step verification, LES resolution acceptance (D*/dx and Pope resolved-TKE tests), and the scope
of applicability of Roache/Richardson grid-convergence-index methods shall follow the current revision of the firm

Document: Units and Conversions Standard Operating Procedure Revision: rev 2 Effective Date: 04/01/2025
Author / Owner: Marguerite Falk, PE — Technical Director & Reviewing Engineer (AZ PE #42798) Applies to: All
engineering analyses, hand calculations, CFD case files, review checklists, memos, and reports produced by The
CFD Mechanical Engineer, LLC. Supersedes: Units and Conversions SOP rev 1.
1. Scope and General Principles
This procedure governs the units in which engineering quantities are computed, recorded, exchanged, and reported
at The CFD ME. It applies to every analyst and reviewer inside the firm, to every contracted CFD hour executed by
third parties on our behalf, and to every artifact — case files, logs, hand-calc worksheets, memos, and client
deliverables — that leaves any engineer's workstation.
The governing principles are three:
SI units shall be used internally throughout all analyses. Reports transmitted to clients working in US customary units
shall include a conversion table in report Section 1. Every numeric value in every artifact shall carry its unit in the
same cell or sentence — a bare number without unit is a defect.
The three principles are jointly binding. Internal SI discipline is not satisfied by a conversion applied at report time; it is
satisfied by keeping the analysis in SI from mesh generation through post-processing so that reviewers see a single
coherent unit system when they audit a case. The conversion table is not optional decoration; on projects whose
client-facing basis is US customary (ASCE 7 wind loads, ASHRAE inputs, Red Butte lab reports quoted in inches and
pounds), the table in Section 1 is the artifact the client uses to cross-read our numbers against their own, and its
absence is grounds for rejection at peer review. The unit-in-the-same-cell rule applies to spreadsheets, CSV column
headers, plot axis labels, memo text, and inline references — no exception is made for "obvious" units or for context
inherited from a section heading.
2. Preferred Units by Quantity
The following preferred units apply to all internal work. Deviations require written justification in the case-setup memo
and reviewer sign-off.

Column headers in CSV and TXT deliverables shall carry the unit in the header string (e.g., T_unexposed_max_C,
pressure_Pa, time_min). Plot axes shall carry the unit in the axis label. Memos and report body prose shall carry
the unit adjacent to every numeric value.
3. Conversions in Routine Use
The following conversions arise routinely in this office's work — ASCE 7-22 wind-load extraction, ASHRAE HVAC
inputs, ASTM E119 lab reports, and construction-industry submittals. The values below are the firm-blessed
conversion factors and shall be used verbatim; do not re-derive from memory at the desk.
•
1 psf = 47.88 Pa
•
1 psi = 6895 Pa
•
1 lb (force) = 4.448 N
•
1 in = 25.4 mm
•
1 ft = 0.3048 m
•
1 BTU/hr·ft² = 3.155 W/m²
•
1 K = 1 °C (for temperature differences only; not for absolute temperatures)
•
T[K] = T[°C] + 273.15 (for absolute temperature conversion)
Two of the above deserve emphasis. First, the psf-to-Pa factor is 47.88, not unity — a psf value carried into a Pa field
without applying the factor is off by nearly two orders of magnitude, which is precisely the failure mode this SOP
exists to prevent. Second, the temperature-difference identity (1 K = 1 °C) applies only to differences; a rise of 139 °C
is a rise of 139 K, but an absolute temperature of 139 °C is 412.15 K, not 139 K.
Additional conversions not listed above shall be sourced from the NIST SP 811 tables and cited by page in the
analyst's worksheet. Conversion factors quoted from web calculators, textbook back-covers, or LLM outputs shall not
be used.
4. Sanity Check Requirement

--- Page 3 ---
Every reported field value shall be sanity-checked against the governing boundary conditions of the load case it
belongs to before rollup. Reviewers shall confirm this check on the peer-review checklist (item 9). A pressure reported
at a scale inconsistent with the case boundary conditions is a defect regardless of unit label.
The check is a scale check, not a unit check. A pressure field whose header reads "Pa" but whose values sit at a
magnitude the boundary conditions cannot produce is defective even if the string "Pa" is technically the intended unit;
the label alone does not vindicate the number. The check is performed at three points in the workflow: (a) by the
case-setup engineer immediately after the first converged or first fully-transient output is produced, (b) by the rollup
engineer at the moment values move from raw fields into summary tables, and (c) by the reviewer at peer review. The
reviewer's confirmation is recorded against item 9 of the peer-review checklist for that project.
Sanity checks are performed against the boundary conditions of the same load case. Cross-case checks are
governed separately by Section 5.
5. Cross-Case Cross-Checks
reported from one case shall not be checked against the boundary conditions of the other.
and their pressure fields are stored in the same case-folder hierarchy. A reviewer who reaches for the wildfire
boundary conditions when sanity-checking a structural wind pressure — or vice versa — will incorrectly clear values
that belong to the other case, or incorrectly flag values that were correct all along. Each case has its own boundary
conditions and its own expected scale, and each is sanity-checked only against its own.
Where a report presents results from both cases, the report body shall separate them under clearly labeled
subheadings and shall not compute or narrate any ratio, difference, or combined figure that would imply a shared
basis.
6. Roles and Sign-Off
•
Analyst (case-setup or rollup engineer): Responsible for enforcing SI-internal discipline at the case level,
populating unit-bearing column headers and cell labels, and performing the Section 4 sanity check at case-output
and rollup.
•
Peer Reviewer (Technical Director or delegated PE): Responsible for confirming item 9 of the peer-review
checklist against the artifact under review; responsible for flagging any unit-bearing defect as a report defect
rather than an editorial comment.
•
Principal Engineer (stamp holder): Responsible for confirming, prior to stamp, that the conversion table is
present in report Section 1 when applicable, and that no bare-number defects remain in the deliverable.
•
Technical Director: Owner of this SOP; responsible for periodic revision, incorporation of lessons learned from
peer-review findings, and dissemination to contracted CFD hours executed on the firm's behalf.
Deviations from this SOP require written approval from the Technical Director in advance of the deviation, recorded in
the project folder.

This is Pope's criterion for a well-resolved LES. The ratio shall be computed on a time-average of a statistically

judgement in place of the numerical evidence; where a physical constraint prevents meeting either criterion, the

6. Reporting
The Verification section of every LES deliverable shall state, directly in the body of the report:
•
The fire heat release rate Q_dot used to compute D*, with units.
•
The characteristic plume diameter D*, with units.
•
The representative cell edge length dx in the region of interest, with units.
•
The plume resolution index D*/dx as a dimensionless number.
•
The Pope resolved-TKE fraction k_res / (k_res + k_sgs) as a percentage, together with the location of the probe(s)
and the length of the averaging window.
These values shall appear in the running text or in a table in the Verification section itself. Placement of any of these

GCI values shall not appear in LES deliverables. A three-grid table copied forward from a RANS template into an
